title: What is refresh-ahead caching (proactively recompute a value in the background shortly before its TTL expires so regularly-accessed keys never miss), and how does probabilistic early recompute spread that refresh load so keys don't all refresh at the same instant?
shortTitle: What is refresh-ahead caching, and how does probabilistic early recompute help?
keyPoints: Refresh-ahead proactively reloads a hot value in the background before its TTL expires, so readers never hit a slow miss.
Caffeine implements this with refreshAfterWrite, which returns the stale value immediately while one background thread reloads.
A cache stampede (thundering herd) happens when many keys expire at the same instant and a flood of readers all reload simultaneously.
Probabilistic early recompute (XFetch) makes each read refresh with a probability that grows as expiry nears, scattering refreshes over a window.
Per-key TTL jitter is the cheapest defense: keys loaded together get slightly different TTLs so they do not expire at once.
Single-flight (one-loader) ensures at most one reload per key, complementing the time-spreading of probabilistic recompute.
Refresh-ahead only warms keys that are actually read, which is correct because there is no point refreshing something nobody wants.

s1_definition.oneliner: Refresh-ahead recomputes a hot value in the background just before its TTL expires so readers never miss, and probabilistic early recompute spreads refreshes over time so keys do not all reload at the same instant and stampede the database.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Refresh-Ahead** – a proactive caching strategy that reloads a popular value in the background before its TTL expires, so readers always hit a fresh cached value and never experience a blocking miss.
- **refreshAfterWrite (Caffeine)** – returns the existing value immediately and triggers an async background reload, unlike expireAfterWrite which blocks on reload.
- **Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd)** – many keys expire at the same instant and all readers simultaneously trigger expensive reloads, overwhelming the database.
- **Probabilistic Early Recompute (XFetch)** – each read refreshes with a probability that rises as expiry nears, scattering refreshes over a window instead of concentrating them at the deadline.
- **TTL Jitter** – adding a small random offset to each key's TTL so a batch of keys does not expire together.
- **Single-Flight** – ensuring only one thread actually performs the reload per key, so concurrent readers share the result.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India the lobby displays today's gold rate computed from a slow external feed, valid for five minutes. With plain expiry, at exactly five minutes the display blanks and the next customer forces the clerk to run the slow computation while everyone waits. Refresh-ahead is the clerk who quietly recomputes in the back office a few seconds early so the screen never goes blank. Probabilistic early recompute is the clever twist: each screen rolls a dice that becomes more likely to say "refresh now" the closer it gets to expiry, so refreshes trickle in spread across the last minute.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Plain Expiry vs Refresh-Ahead
  ─────────────────────────────

  Plain Expiry:
  ┌─────────┐     TTL expires     ┌──────────┐
  │ Cached  │────────────────────►│ EXPIRED  │
  │ (fast)  │                     │ next read│
  └─────────┘                     │ BLOCKS   │
                                  └──────────┘

  Refresh-Ahead:
  ┌─────────┐  near TTL, bg refresh  ┌──────────┐
  │ Cached  │────────────────────────►│ Refreshed│
  │ (fast)  │  reader gets stale val  │ (fresh)  │
  └─────────┘  instantly, no block    └──────────┘


  Probabilistic Early Recompute
  ─────────────────────────────
  Time ──────────────────────────────────► Expiry
  │                                        │
  │  P(refresh) ≈ 0    P(refresh) grows    │
  │  ·····          ·····  ////  █████████ │
  │                                        │
  Refreshes scattered     Not all at once
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Refresh-ahead caching proactively reloads a popular value in the background before its TTL expires, so readers always get a fast hit and never experience a blocking miss. Caffeine implements this with refreshAfterWrite, which returns the stale value immediately while one background thread reloads, unlike expireAfterWrite which blocks the reader.

The danger is the cache stampede: if many keys share the same expiry, they all expire at once and a flood of readers simultaneously hammers the database. Probabilistic early recompute (XFetch) solves this by making each read refresh with a probability that rises as expiry nears, scattering refreshes over a window. Per-key TTL jitter is the cheapest complement, and single-flight ensures only one thread actually reloads per key.

Refresh-ahead trades a little freshness for zero latency, which is the right trade for a displayed aggregate but never for an authoritative balance used to approve a debit. It also only warms keys that are actually read, which is correct because there is no point refreshing something nobody wants.

Remember one sentence: refresh-ahead keeps hot keys always fresh by reloading in the background before TTL expires, and probabilistic early recompute plus jitter prevent the synchronized stampede.
